title: Uns al-Wujud and Rose-In-Hood (简体中文)

full_text:
Uns al-Wujud was a noble youth of Isfahan, renowned for his martial prowess, his gentle manners, and his mastery of verse. He loved Al-Ward fi'l-Akmam—whose name meant 'Rose-in-Hood'—the daughter of the Grand Vizier. Their affection was celebrated across the city for its pure nobility, but the proud vizier, fearing court gossip, secretly transported his daughter to the Castle of the Mountain of Birds, an inaccessible fortress perched on a sea-girt island.

Devastated by her disappearance, Uns al-Wujud cast off his armor, donned a pilgrim’s cloak, and set forth alone into the wilderness to find his bride.

For months, he wandered through scorching deserts and rocky ravines, speaking only to the wild beasts and reciting poems of longing to the wind. Seeing his pure heart and unyielding devotion, the wild gazelles walked beside him, and a friendly hermit of the mountains gave him shelter, pointing him toward the Sea of Birds.

Reaching the rocky coast, an old boatman was so moved by the youth’s verses that he rowed him across the stormy straits to the island fortress.

Meanwhile, Rose-in-Hood sat upon the battlements, releasing carrier pigeons with inscribed verses of hope. One pigeon landed upon Uns al-Wujud's shoulder as he climbed the rocky crags.

Recognizing her beloved’s voice as he sang below the walls, Rose-in-Hood lowered silk cords from her balcony, and the lovers were joyfully reunited.

When the vizier arrived with armed troops to punish the intruder, he heard the young couple reciting their sublime poems of fidelity. His stern heart melted with remorse. He embraced Uns al-Wujud as his worthy son, gave them his blessing, and celebrated a magnificent wedding in Isfahan that became a legend of true love across the East.
moral: Enduring devotion, poetry, and compassionate friendship conquer deserts, mountains, and separation. [ZH]
